opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it changed my view quite a lot, though maybe not in the direction people expect.

Before we trained it, I was still somewhat of a believer in the simple story: you scale up parameters, you scale up data, the loss goes down smoothly, and capability more or less follows. And at the level of the loss curve, that story still holds. The scaling behavior was very predictable. That part wasn't surprising.

What surprised me was how loosely loss and "capability" were coupled once you got to that size. Some things that we expected to improve a lot, like multi-step reasoning or the model holding a consistent line of thought over a long problem, improved much less than the loss reduction would suggest. Meanwhile, knowledge breadth, fluency, and long-tail recall improved enormously. So I started to think of parameter scale as mostly buying you *memory* and *coverage*, a much bigger compressed picture of the world, but not automatically buying you better *thinking*.

The second lesson was about cost. At a trillion parameters, every mistake in the data mixture or in the training recipe is extremely expensive, and you can't iterate the way you do with smaller models. That pushed us to do much more of the real research at smaller scale and treat the big run almost as an engineering execution. It made me realize that the research frontier and the scale frontier are not the same place.

And the third thing, which is maybe the most important for how I think now: after that model, I became much more convinced that the next big gains come from what happens after pretraining. Reinforcement learning, letting the model generate long reasoning chains and learn from feedback, that's where we saw capability jump in ways that more parameters alone didn't give us. The big pretrained model is a very good foundation, a very rich prior, but it's the training on top of it that turns knowledge into ability.

So if I summarize: scale is still necessary, I don't think anyone should pretend otherwise. But it's no longer sufficient, and I think the field spent a little too long believing that it was.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that model was the thing that shook my confidence in pure scaling more than anything else. Going in, I was a true believer. My whole intuition from the vision days was that if you fix the data and the recipe and just make the model bigger, you get better on basically everything. And for a long stretch that was exactly what we saw. Knowledge-type questions, language understanding, writing, everything kept climbing with size.

But when we got to the trillion-parameter range, we saw something I didn't expect. On reasoning tasks, especially math, the bigger model wasn't better. In some settings it was actually worse than a smaller model trained on the same data. That was very hard to accept at first. We spent a long time checking whether it was a bug, a data issue, an evaluation artifact. It wasn't.

What I eventually came to believe is that scale is really good at one thing, which is compression. A larger model memorizes and interpolates the distribution of the data more faithfully. For knowledge, that's exactly what you want. For reasoning, it can be the wrong objective. The bigger model learns to reproduce the surface pattern of a solution, the way a human would write it down, instead of the actual process of getting there. A smaller model, almost by necessity, can't memorize as much, so it's sometimes forced to learn something closer to the underlying procedure. So you end up with this paradox where more capacity gives you more imitation and less thinking.

That reframed the whole question for me. Scale is still necessary. I don't think you get frontier capability without it. But it stopped being sufficient in my mind. The missing piece wasn't more parameters, it was changing what the model is optimizing for, letting it generate its own intermediate steps and get feedback on whether they actually work rather than whether they look like the training text. That's roughly why I became so focused on reinforcement learning and long chains of reasoning afterward. The trillion-parameter run didn't fail in a dramatic way. It just quietly told me that the thing I thought was one axis is really two.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about treating the parameter count itself as an explanation of capability. The important question is what additional scale lets a model learn—and whether the data, training process, and evaluation are good enough to make that visible.

A larger model can have more capacity, but that doesn’t automatically mean better reasoning or more reliable answers. You need to distinguish improvements on familiar tasks from the ability to generalize to unfamiliar ones.

So I’d frame the relationship this way: scale creates an opportunity for greater capability. Realizing that opportunity is a whole-system problem. And demonstrating it requires more than pointing to the size of the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about treating parameter count as a direct measure of capability. A trillion parameters describes scale, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell you what a model can reliably do. You have to look at the quality of the data, how effectively the model is trained, and how you evaluate it.

So the distinction I’d make is between capacity and realized capability. Scale creates room for improvement; it doesn’t guarantee that you’ve used that room well. The meaningful question is whether the additional scale produces useful, consistent gains on the tasks you care about.
